title: Test Vectors — RFC / NIST CAVP Workflow

questions.question: What is a cryptographic test vector?
options: A published input/output pair that fixes behavior byte-for-byte
A random sample used only to estimate performance and throughput
A secret key that must be kept private to preserve security guarantees
A graph of algorithm complexity as input size increases in theory
questions.explanation: Test vectors are deterministic examples (often from RFC/NIST sources) that define exact expected behavior for interoperability.

questions.question: Why is it risky to have only happy-path vectors for a parser or decoder?
options: A wrong parser may still pass while accepting malformed or ambiguous inputs
The implementation will always run slower and use more memory
The code becomes constant-time by accident and hides timing bugs
The vectors will stop matching whenever the compiler updates
questions.explanation: Many real crypto bugs are about what you accept. Without negative vectors, incorrect acceptance can go unnoticed.

questions.question: In this repo, what are the two required top-level keys in `tests/vectors.json`?
options: `source` and `vectors`
`title` and `examples`
`inputs` and `outputs`
`seed` and `cases`
questions.explanation: Every vectors file includes a citation string in `source` and a list of vector objects in `vectors`.

questions.question: For a single vector entry, which rule best matches the harness pattern used in this repo?
options: It includes an `op` plus exactly one of `expected` or `expected_error`
It includes an `op` and must include both `expected` and `expected_error`
It includes no `op` and relies on test order to choose behavior at runtime
It includes only `expected` and generates random inputs inside the test code
questions.explanation: Vectors are dispatched by `op`, and each one asserts either a successful result or a required rejection.

questions.question: Why does this repo prefer `msg_hex` fields for byte strings in vectors?
options: Hex removes ambiguity about bytes, encodings, and hidden Unicode changes
Hex is always shorter than ASCII and reduces file size significantly
Hex guarantees the code is constant-time even for parsing routines
Hex prevents collisions for hashes by changing the digest function
questions.explanation: Using hex makes the exact bytes explicit and avoids accidental text/Unicode transformations at the boundary.

questions.question: What does a negative test vector assert?
options: The implementation must reject a specific malformed input
The implementation must produce a different output on each run
The implementation must always use a random nonce internally
The implementation must be faster than a reference library
questions.explanation: Negative vectors encode “MUST reject” rules: malformed inputs should fail in a predictable way.

questions.question: Which mistake can make vectors appear to pass while hashing the wrong thing?
options: Hashing the characters of a hex string instead of decoding hex to bytes first
Computing the digest in lowercase instead of uppercase hex formatting
Using a list of vectors instead of a dictionary of named vectors
Printing the digest to the console before comparing it to expected
questions.explanation: If vectors store bytes as hex, your code must decode the hex to bytes before hashing or signing; otherwise you test a different message.

questions.question: Which broken implementation is most likely to slip through if vectors lack hostile edge cases?
options: A decoder that accepts non-canonical encodings and never rejects malformed inputs
A decoder that uses the same error type for all failures and exits early
A decoder that allocates memory proportional to the input length and returns
A decoder that prints debug output for each parsed block and continues
questions.explanation: Edge cases and negative vectors are what catch incorrect acceptance behavior, which is a common source of crypto vulnerabilities.
